One of the things the data analysts on our side obsessed over was "composition"—whether the electorate looked close enough to 2024 for Republicans to win. And despite polls that showed a Democrat blowout, the data kept on telling us the same story: in some states turnout was merely OK, in other states it was downright amazing, and in no state was it catastrophic. There was a genuine sense of optimism on our team: our people were showing up. 

So, I asked the smartest data guy I know, does that mean we're going to shock the world? "No," he told me. "We might do better than the polls suggest. But the data is telling us that a lot of Trump/Vance 2024 voters are pissed and planning to vote for the other guys. Our voters are turning out, but they may not vote for us."

Well, that looks prophetic now. Our voters did show up. In Florida, for example, the electorate was 9 points more Republican than Democrat, just a couple points worse than 2024. Undoubtedly there were places we could have done better on turnout. But the main problem is not turnout. The main problem is that many people who voted for Trump/Vance in 2024 voted for Democrats in 2026. 

There will be a lot of infighting and arguing over what happened and why that is. One of the pollsters I really respect told me that our economic messaging wasn’t sharp enough down the stretch. I’m sure that’s true. 

But the real reason we lost is obvious to almost everyone. 

Another pollster—one of the smartest people I know in politics, told me yesterday we’d lose the generic ballot by 13 points. I felt negative going into Tuesday, but even I was shocked by this. In his polling, he saw that a lot of Trump 2024 voters were angry and planning to vote for Democrats. He asked those voters who had abandoned us what would cause them to come back on our team. The top four answers, accounting for nearly all of the responses were:

1) End the war
2) Focus on cost of living/inflation
3) Put America First
4) Change our relationship to Israel

Our voters showed up. And the above four reasons are why many of them voted for Democrats. This is according to a pollster who nailed the results. While many spent Monday attacking Rachel Campos Duffy for calling for a diplomatic resolution to the conflict, it turns out her political advice was sound. (She’s also a great person.)

In the next few months, there's going to be a lot of gaslighting. Expect to hear any number of establishment politicians say the solution to our woes is amnesty. I'm open to the idea that we should change enforcement—by focusing more on businesses that hire illegal labor, for instance. But anyone pushing amnesty is lying to you. 

The reason we lost is the war. The president himself said so last night. 

If you'd like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so. Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay. Agree or disagree, that's at least honest.

But everyone knows why we lost. And any honest conversation about where we go from here must start there.

I remain hopeful about our country. To the people who are pissed off and want to say, “I told you so”: you’re right, you did tell us so. Take that energy into electing Republicans who share your worldview. To the people who are just pissed at the results, you should be. Let’s take that anger and get back to the work of saving our country.

items.tx:
History was made last night.

For months, we were saying that 2026 was the most consequential midterm election of our lifetimes. 

Unfortunately, we were right. Sometimes history is to be celebrated; other times, it is to be mourned. Always, it must be reckoned with.

2026 was not simply a blue wave; it was a blue tsunami. It was an ass kicking. It was not simply a bad 2006 midterm election. It was a Watergate-level repudiation. What happened, and why? What are the consequences, and where on earth do we go from here?

When all the votes were counted, the problem wasn’t turnout. Instead, our voters, Republicans, Libertarians, Independents, showed up and voted, and rejected our candidates, voting Democrat instead. We’ve lost the House. We’ve lost the Senate. When all is said and done, we will have lost eight to 10 Senate seats.

We lost in historically red states, like South Carolina and North Carolina, Kansas and Iowa. We lost in purple states, like Michigan, and New Hampshire, and Georgia. And we just barely won by just a single point in bright red states like Florida and Louisiana, and then there’s Texas.

Nowhere are the consequences of this election greater than Texas. In the Lone Star State, we lost every single statewide election. For weeks, I had been publicly warning on this podcast that we were in very real danger of losing everything in Texas. Far too few believed that was possible. I am very, very sorry that it came to pass. Texas has not had a Democrat governor since 1994. We haven’t had a Democrat senator since 1993. Now we’ll have both.

Why were the results so overwhelming? Pundits and analysts will break down the results for weeks or months or even years to come, but several things are already evident today.

Years ago, the very best political advice I ever got was from Heidi. She said, “It’s not about you. It’s about them. It’s about their kids, their families, their hopes, their dreams, their futures.” Too many politicians forget that.

Take the state of Kansas, for example, a state that has not elected a Democrat senator since 1932. It just did. Here’s what exit polling showed were the top issues in Kansas.

Number one, cost of living, energy, and groceries. That was listed as number one by 30.6 percent of voters. 
Corruption. Number two, 18.5%. 
The cost of the Iran war, 10.1%. 
The candidates are terrible, 7.9%. 
The Canada trade war, 7.6%. 
The GOP didn’t do enough to support Trump, 6.6%. 
Republicans didn’t pass the Save America Act, 5.6%. 
Trump’s focus on monuments, 5.5%, and data centers and AI, 3.8%.

The top issue, cost of living, is very real. Too many in politics dismissed it. They didn’t understand. They pointed to the macro numbers showing the stock markets soaring, median income at record highs, and poverty at record lows. Those data are true, but they don’t tell all of the story.

Here are some stats that are a lot more real and personal. Spam, Hormel’s processed meat substitute, broke record sales, selling 113 million cans last year. That is nearly as much spam as was sold during the entirety of World War II. 29 percent of Americans have used buy now, pay later for groceries this year. That’s double the share just two years ago.

In August, banks repossessed 42% more homes than they did last year. In 2024, car repossessions topped 2.3 million, above the 2009 peak in the middle of the Great Financial Crisis. In 2025, 6% of 401k holders took hardship withdrawals, paying penalties. That is a record, and triple the norm.

And here’s one that’s really stunning. Americans made more than 75 million paid plasma donations in 2026. That’s another record. That means 200,000 Americans every single day, with a needle in their arm, just to pay for groceries.

That is very real pain from real Americans, and too many Republican politicians seem like they didn’t understand or they didn’t care. Food is too high, gas is too high, diesel is too high, insurance is too high, life is too high.

I don't claim to be an expert in human behavior, but I've watched Trump for 11 years now, and I'm pretty good at pattern recognition.

items.t: BREAKING: HOLY SMOKES! Democrats now control enough states to effectively abolish the Electoral College through the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact. R
items.tx:
BREAKING: HOLY SMOKES! Democrats now control enough states to effectively abolish the Electoral College through the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact.

Republicans did NOT have this on their bingo cards...

Under the Constitution, states control their electoral votes and are allowed to decide how they are allocated during presidential elections. Currently, almost every state gives its votes to whoever wins the state.

In practice, the current system means that a candidate can win the national popular vote, but lose the election because small states like Wyoming exert undue influence on the outcome. That state has 3 electoral votes with a population of just 577,000 people. California has 54 electoral votes and a population of 39.5 million people. So a vote in Wyoming is essentially 3.8 times as valuable as one in California.

Since 1992, Democrats have won the popular vote seven out of nine times.

Under the NPV, states that join agree to give their electoral votes to whoever wins the national popular vote, not just their own state. So a state could go red on the map, but if the Democrat wins the national vote, they still get that state's votes. And vice versa of course.

The crucial mechanism is that the compact doesn't trigger until the member states have a combined power of at least 270 electoral votes, the number needed to win the White House. So far, 18 states plus D.C. have joined, totaling 222 electoral votes. We only need 48 more.

Now is the chance to pass this measure in every state possible. Democrats won both houses of the legislature in Wisconsin for the first time in 18 years (10 electoral votes). We won the Pennsylvania state Senate for the first time since 1993 (19 votes). We now have a trifecta in Michigan (15 votes). And we won the governor’s race in Nevada (6 votes).

10 + 19 + 15 + 6 = 50. 

222 + 50 = 272.

And if we hold our lead in the Arizona Senate, that number could climb as high as 283, more than enough to trigger the compact.

In addition to removing an imbalance in our system that favors Republicans, this novel approach would fundamentally change how candidates run their presidential campaigns. Currently, they are incentivized to ignore most of the country. If you live in a “safe” state, red or blue, your vote for President is basically decided before you cast it. Campaigns spend their time and money in a handful of swing states while the rest of us watch from the sidelines. If the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact is adopted, they'll have reason to hit every state because they're aiming to win the largest swath of the country as a whole, not just certain states.

States have until July 20, 2028 to join the compact in time for the next presidential election.

We can fix our democracy. The time is now.

Please ❤️ and share if you support this idea!

Extraordinarily, Scott Colom is on track to win the uncalled Senate race in Mississippi (the last margin I saw was 39 votes but the remaining count favours him, as Kornacki shows in this clip).

My election observations... I'm titling it... "The Rope-a-Dope"... 

Trump is leaning against the ropes, congratulating the people throwing punches at him, while an entirely different fight unfolds around the ring...

Three days before the midterms, Trump posted Muhammad Ali's 1971 defeat against Joe Frazier... that caught my attention because Ali's greatest strategic masterpiece came three years later against George Foreman... the rope-a-dope...

Ali absorbed punishment against the ropes, allowing Foreman to exhaust himself while the crowd watched what appeared to be a losing fighter... then, in the eighth round, Ali came off those ropes and knocked Foreman out...

Now look at November 3... Dems capture Congress, the media celebrates, and Trump congratulates his opponents, praises their performance, and offers cooperation...

He distances himself from the losses, reminding everyone he wasn't on the ballot and still possesses presidential veto authority...

See the positioning? He's absorbing the blows while his opponents inherit responsibility for what follows...

Meanwhile another sequence was unfolding... in September, DOJ issued litigation holds covering election records in 29 states and Washington, D.C. On October 26, Trump announced a proposed $1 million election fraud reward, alongside DOJ's separate $10,000 to $30,000 fraud incentive program...

On October 29, DOJ reinforced the 22-month federal election record preservation requirement, warning against deliberate destruction... 

Then just one day before the election, a Michigan judge permanently blocked deletion of original electronic pollbooks after certification, preserving underlying data and metadata... "watch Michigan"...

Election evidence was being legally protected before the outcome was known...

Simultaneously ~1,000 DOJ monitors and observers covered 126 jurisdictions across all 50 states...

Hegseth mobilized military intelligence, Cyber Command, and the NSA against foreign interference, while DOJ's voter registration litigation tested federal authority against state sovereignty and privacy protections...

Election Day produced localized scanner failures, ballot shortages, bomb threats, and disruptions. Federal cyber monitoring reported limited threats and no identified foreign influence operations by late election night... preserved records now provide a foundation for lawful audits and investigations...

Zoom out and connect the systems... federal monitoring expanded as courts enforced constitutional boundaries... cyber defenses operated alongside evidence preservation... Congressional power shifted while the presidency retained its executive authority... and Trump is congratulating the Democrats...

Ali understood this dynamic... Foreman's aggression, confidence, and energy expenditure became variables influencing the fight... the punches were landing while conditions for Ali's counterattack developed...

Trump's Ali posts, his election response, and the institutional activity surrounding November 3 create a striking parallel...

The congressional defeat is real, legal processes continue, election records remain preserved, and Trump retains his constitutional powers...

Trump has absorbed the immediate political damage while positioning himself for the next phase...

Some of my immediate takeaways from the midterms:

1. This wasn’t a blue wave. This wasn’t even a blue tsunami. This was a blue mass extinction event. The Republican coalition which seemingly gave Trump a mandate 2 years ago fell apart everywhere, on all sides. There was a big polling error, but what happened is that polls underestimated Democrats. The generic ballot will seemingly end at D+13. This goes above and beyond what the rosiest Dem forecasts thought could happen. 
2. Trumpism has been conclusively smashed at the polls, not even just Trump himself. The Rust Belt didn’t have any sympathy for tariffs, hawkish voters had no sympathy for the Iran War, and non-college educated whites had no sympathy for the attacks on colleges and mass ICE raids. Republicans might’ve lost young men for a generation. All types of Republicans across the country faced the wrath of voters. The GOP has been completely transformed into MAGA’s fashion, but that will be a detriment for voters. Turns out, Trump only broke the laws of political gravity when he had the benefit of the doubt regarding a (relatively) peaceful world and a good economy. 
3. Zohran Mamdani is the most influential Dem politician of the decade already. His message, though very much altered for different states and different candidates, became the Democratic Party’s midterm platform. The idea that Mamdani would be some fringe figure in the Dem coalition, as proffered by some pundits last year, has been thoroughly disproven. He will be only next to Obama and Bernie as the models for all Dem politicians, particularly on the left, going forward
4. Israel took a drubbing at the polls. The Iran War created the high gas prices and inflation that drew the floor out from underneath the GOP coalition. We already know how Dem voters view Israel as being the worst thing on Earth. But now Republicans (even JD Vance as we’ve seen today) are also mad at Israel for pushing them into a war that’s remarkably unpopular, and that America will ultimately lose. The GOP will continue to be institutionally pro-Israel, due to donors and other factors, but GOP politicians and particularly pollsters now view Israel as a liability, both personally and politically. 
5. The effect on the 2028 Dem primary sweepstakes is as such: Josh Shapiro’s case is over (why would Dems care about nominating an electorally skillful moderate after THIS kind of anti-GOP drubbing?), Gavin Newsom might now just become irrelevant, and the stock of such characters as Mark Kelly, Ro Khanna, Andy Beshear, Elissa Slotkin, Cory Booker, Jared Polis, Gretchen Whitmer, and Pete Buttigieg has gone down (Chris Murphy’s stock has also gone down too, for other reasons). Kamala Harris’ stock has gone up, as Dems now begin to feel that Kamala’s loss has been properly avenged and she can now start planning her reconquest. James Talarico is ascendant (Beto had a serious 2020 campaign just by *barely losing* a Texas senate seat, and a Dem Texas Governor removes the issue of losing his senate seat to the GOP), and AOC had her best night possible. Primary voters will now care less about electability, and care more about totally repudiating Trumpism and policy. Those are the lanes progressives do best in. AOC, even she prefers to become a Senator, is now positioned to be the Barry Goldwater or even Ronald Reagan of the Dem left. But the best night goes to Jon Ossoff. 18 point victory in a swing state. He is now the frontrunner, no ifs or buts.
